shippingNews.postTitle: R/V Neil Armstrong Heads for Great Lakes

stories.body: The R/V Neil Armstrong departed its home port of Woods Hole, Massachusetts, on Wednesday, October 28. It will travel from Cape Cod down the St. Lawrence Seaway, through the locks, and across the Great Lakes. The 238-foot vessel is expected to arrive in Duluth on November 9. R/V Neil Armstrong is Great Lakes-bound. As of Thursday morning, the Neil Armstrong was traveling up the Atlantic Coast around Nova Scotia. todayInHistory.title: Sam Laud
todayInHistory.text: Sam Laud Bay Shipbuilding Corp. of Sturgeon Bay, WI, laid the keel for their hull # 712 on Jan. 4, 1974 to be built as a smaller-sized Great Lakes self-unloading bulk cargo carrier. The new vessel was launched on Nov. 19, 1974 for Buffalo's American Steamship Co. (ASC), a subsidiary of GATX Corp., Chicago, IL. Completed in 1975, the self-unloader was christened Sam Laud by Mrs. Edna Laud on behalf of her husband at a christening ceremony held April 15, 1975. Mr. Laud was the former president (1945) and chairman of the board (1956) of GATX Corp., having started with the company in 1916 as shop painter and riveter. Mr. Laud died August 1, 1963. GATX Corp. had acquired ASC in July of 1973. Mrs. Laud was accompanied by Mr. Frederick G. Jaicks, chairman and CEO of Inland Steel Co., Chicago, IL, who gave the address at the christening ceremonies. One of a new generation of self-unloaders for the ASC fleet, the Sam Laud was built at an approximate cost of $13.3 million and was the fourth of 10 self-unloaders launched for the fleet under Chapter XI of the Merchant Marine Act of 1970. Under this act, the U.S. government-guaranteed financing and tax deferred benefits for fleet modernizing. The other ASC self-unloaders built under this program were the Roger M. Kyes (now Adam E. Cornelius, 1973), Charles E. Wilson (now John J. Boland, 1973), H. Lee White (1974), St. Clair (1976), Belle River (now Walter J. marineWeather.synopsis: A 30.3 inch high stretching from Alberta to the Upper Great Lakes this morning will continue building to 30.4 inches over the Upper Great Lakes today. High pressure then shifts to the Lower Great Lakes by Saturday morning and strengthens to 30.5 inches, with ridging of around 30.2 inches lingering over Lake Superior through the weekend as the high gradually shifts to the Eastern Seaboard. A 29.6 inch Colorado low develops on Monday and moves into Minnesota by Tuesday morning. This low passes north of Lake Superior into northern Ontario Tuesday night at 29.5 inches, dragging troughing of at least 29.6 inches over the western half of the lake Tuesday into Wednesday.

High pressure around 30.4 inches will work its way across the Upper Great Lakes Region today with winds turning more northeasterly and lessening as it moves over Lake Michigan. Then winds become southeasterly later tonight as high pressure slowly exits. Moderate southeasterly winds return for Saturday as low pressure around 29.8 inches moves into the central Plains. Light to moderate southeasterly to southerly winds then persist into Monday, increasing for Tuesday as low pressure approaches. Gales may be possible at times early next week.

Brisk northwest flow this morning continues across Lake Huron in the wake of a cold front. High pressure, 30.40 inches, will then build in tonight and through the weekend, relaxing wind speeds and bringing in a period of lighter winds.

Behind a departing cold front this morning, high pressure 30.40 inches will build southeast over the area and persist into the weekend. A warm front will lift north across the lake on Sunday into Sunday night. The area will linger in the warm sector into the start of next week.

A 30.4 inch high will settle over the lower Great Lakes tonight. This high will then drift to the eastern seaboard Tuesday, then east of the Mid Atlantic coast by Wednesday. Meanwhile, a 29.3 inch low over far northwest Ontario province Tuesday night will move to Hudson Bay by late Wednesday, then to northern Quebec by Thursday while deepening to 29.0 inches. A trailing cold front will cross the lower Great Lakes Wednesday night, with a 30.0 inch high building east across the eastern Great Lakes region Thursday through Friday, before sliding east into New England by Saturday.
